Program Identity

Research Mission

The program develops engineering capability in CanSat, model rocketry, avionics, telemetry, digital twins and satellite systems through requirements-driven design, simulation, prototyping, testing and measured experimentation.

Why This Program

It is an engineering, experimentation and research-oriented program, not only a training course. Learners are expected to justify design decisions with requirements, analysis and measured data, and to document them the way aerospace projects do.

Understand the physics. Engineer the system. Build it. Test it. Fly it. Analyse it.

Five Kinds of Work

Not every activity is research, and the program does not present it that way. It distinguishes five kinds of work:

Learning
Fundamentals of flight, electronics, programming and systems engineering.
Engineering development
Requirements, architecture, budgets, design baselines and reviews.
Experimentation
Planned tests on prototypes, with measured results.
Research
Open questions investigated with models and data. Research outputs are still developing.
Flight validation
Comparing predicted and measured flight performance, only where an authorised flight takes place.

The Engineering Loop

Learners progress through the same loop on every design iteration:

  1. 1Model
  2. 2Simulate
  3. 3Design
  4. 4Build
  5. 5Test
  6. 6Measure
  7. 7Analyse
  8. 8Improve
    , then back to Model

Engineering Review Gates

Eight Reviews, One Question Each

A gate is a decision point. Work does not move to the next stage until the review question can be answered with evidence.

  1. MCRQ1

    Mission Concept Review

    Is the mission concept clear, feasible and worth pursuing?

  2. SRRQ1

    System Requirements Review

    Are the system requirements complete, consistent and verifiable?

  3. PDRQ2

    Preliminary Design Review

    Does the preliminary design meet the requirements within its mass, power and data budgets?

  4. CDRQ3

    Critical Design Review

    Is the detailed design mature enough to build and integrate?

  5. TRRQ3

    Test Readiness Review

    Are the system, the procedures and the team ready to test safely?

  6. FRRQ4

    Flight Readiness Review

    Do the vehicle, payload, procedures and compliance evidence support an authorised flight?

  7. ORRQ4

    Operational Readiness Review

    Educational systems-engineering review

    Are the operating procedures, roles and ground systems ready?

  8. FinalQ4

    Final Research Review

    What was learned, and does the measured evidence support it?

Review names follow common systems-engineering practice, as described in the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook(opens in a new tab).

Core Theme

Digital Twin Engineering

A model is only as good as its agreement with measurement. Digital-twin work in the program means building a model, testing the real system, and using the difference between the two to improve both.

  1. 1Model
  2. 2Simulate
  3. 3Build
  4. 4Test
  5. 5Compare
  6. 6Calibrate
  7. 7Improve

CubeTwin is a digital engineering / digital-twin learning platform used to model and analyse mission behaviour before and after physical testing. It is an educational prototype that works with simulated data and is not flight software.

CubeTwin(opens in a new tab)

Predicted vs Measured

Illustrative
  • Predicted
  • Measured
Predicted Apogee
1,020 m
Measured Apogee
947 m
Difference
7.2%

Why?

  • Drag coefficient
  • Actual vehicle mass
  • Wind
  • Motor thrust curve
  • Launch angle
  • Sensor error

Each candidate cause can be checked against measured data. That is why flight logs, telemetry and test records matter as much as the hardware.

Research Directions

Example Research Questions

These are example research directions that learners may investigate. They are not claims of completed research.

  1. 01How does fin geometry affect stability, drag and achievable altitude?
  2. 02How accurately can low-cost sensors reconstruct flight state?
  3. 03How does telemetry packet loss vary with altitude, orientation and distance?
  4. 04How accurately does simulation predict actual apogee?
  5. 05How can recovery-system parameters minimise landing velocity while managing drift?
  6. 06How does temperature influence onboard battery performance during a flight?
  7. 07Can sensor fusion improve altitude and attitude estimation?
  8. 08Can telemetry anomalies be detected automatically?
  9. 09How closely can a digital twin reproduce measured flight behaviour?
Mandatory

Safety & Regulatory Compliance

Any physical model-rocketry, CanSat deployment, launch, recovery, radio / telemetry or field-testing activity must be conducted only under applicable laws, regulatory guidance, authorised venue / range conditions, competent supervision and documented safety procedures.

From design to authorised activity

  1. 1Design
  2. 2Safety Review
  3. 3Compliance Review
  4. 4Test Readiness
  5. 5Flight Readiness
  6. 6Authorised Activity
  7. 7Post-Flight Review

Propulsion is taught as an educational, safety-oriented subject: approved educational and commercially appropriate propulsion systems, safe engineering practice and competition-rule compliance. The program does not cover propellant formulation or motor manufacturing.

Where applicable, consider:

  • IN-SPACe / Department of Space guidance
  • Venue and range permissions
  • Applicable aviation / airspace requirements
  • Radio-frequency regulations
  • Electrical and battery safety
  • Fire safety
  • Recovery-zone safety
  • Weather limits
  • Emergency procedures

Requirements are set by the relevant authorities, venues and organisers. Official sources:

  • IN-SPACe(opens in a new tab)
  • ISRO, Department of Space(opens in a new tab)

FAQ

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the CanSat & Model Rocketry Engineering Research Program?

It is a 12-month engineering, experimentation and research-oriented program from THASMAI Space Research covering CanSat, model rocketry, avionics, telemetry, digital twins and satellite engineering foundations. Learners progress through requirements-driven design, simulation, prototyping, testing and measured experimentation.

Is it a research program or a training program?

It is research-oriented, and it is explicit about the difference. The program distinguishes learning, engineering development, experimentation, research and flight validation. Research outputs are still developing, and nothing is described as completed research unless it is published and linked.

Who can join?

The program is intended for B.E. / B.Tech and M.E. / M.Tech students in electronics, electrical, mechanical, aerospace, computer science and information technology. It is also suitable for faculty mentors, research interns, student engineering teams and early-career engineers. Eligibility and intake for each cohort are confirmed by the program lead.

How long is the program?

12 months. It runs as an annual cycle from January to December, organised into four quarters.

When was the program started?

The program was initiated on 01 December 2025. The first structured cohort is the 2026 cohort, running from 01 January 2026 to 30 December 2026.

What happens during Q1, Q2, Q3 and Q4?

Q1 (January to March) covers foundations and mission definition, closing with the Mission Concept Review and System Requirements Review. Q2 (April to June) covers architecture and preliminary design, closing with the Preliminary Design Review. Q3 (July to September) covers detailed design, build and integration, with the Critical Design Review and Test Readiness Review. Q4 (October to December) covers flight, validation and research output, with the Flight Readiness Review, an educational Operational Readiness Review and the Final Research Review.

Will students build a real CanSat?

A CanSat prototype is part of the Q3 plan. The Build a CanSat workshop covers the mechanical structure, flight computer, sensors, power, telemetry, payload, firmware, recovery system and ground station, and an integrated prototype is one of the planned Q3 engineering outputs.

Will students build a model rocket?

A model rocket prototype is part of the Q3 plan. The Build a Model Rocket workshop covers the airframe, nose cone, fins, stability, recovery system, payload bay and CanSat integration. Propulsion is covered as an educational, safety-oriented subject using approved educational and commercially appropriate systems.

How is safety handled?

Any physical model-rocketry, CanSat deployment, launch, recovery, radio or field-testing activity must be conducted only under applicable laws, regulatory guidance, authorised venue or range conditions, competent supervision and documented safety procedures. Work passes a safety review and a compliance review before test readiness and flight readiness.

Does the program prepare students for IN-SPACe competitions?

The program builds competition readiness: the technical, documentation, teamwork, mission-design and flight-readiness skills that student aerospace competitions require. Students may have opportunities to prepare for and participate in relevant IN-SPACe competitions, subject to the official competition announcement, team eligibility, institution requirements, application and selection, current-year rules and safety requirements. THASMAI is an independent organisation and does not conduct IN-SPACe competitions.

Can students participate in international competitions?

Potential competition pathways depend on current eligibility rules. Not all international competitions are open to Indian teams, and international participation is not promised. International competitions are referenced as benchmarks for engineering practice.

Is competition participation guaranteed?

No. Participation depends on eligibility, registration, selection, competition rules and organiser schedules. The program focuses on competition readiness.

What is CubeTwin?

CubeTwin is a digital engineering / digital-twin learning platform used to model and analyse mission behaviour before and after physical testing. It is an educational prototype that works with simulated data and is not flight software.

What are the career and research pathways?

The program builds skills relevant to satellite engineering, space systems engineering, avionics, telemetry, embedded systems, ground systems, mission operations, digital twins, aerospace cybersecurity, research and higher studies, and space-tech startups. These are possible pathways, not placement or employment commitments.

How can I know the program fees?

Program fees are not published on this page. Contact the program lead, Sudarshana Karkala, for program details and fees.

Who is the program lead?

Sudarshana Karkala, Co-Founder & Executive Director of THASMAI INFOTECH PRIVATE LIMITED, is the program lead and contact person.
